claims.text: The as-deposited HEA multilayer coatings have well-defined nanoscale architectures.
The as-deposited HEA multilayer coatings contain processing-induced residual stresses.
Decreasing individual layer thickness while retaining the same total stack dimensions increases interface density.
Higher interface density increases barriers to dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion limits the accumulation of time-dependent plastic strain.
Limiting time-dependent plastic strain reduces creep rates.
Limiting time-dependent plastic strain reduces stress-relaxation rates.
Thinner-layer HEA multilayer coatings will have lower creep rates than thicker-layer multilayers or homogeneous HEA coatings.
Thinner-layer HEA multilayer coatings will accumulate less strain than thicker-layer multilayers or homogeneous HEA coatings.
Interface-mediated dislocation impediment is expected to dominate under moderately elevated temperatures and constant loads where creep is active.
Alternative deformation mechanisms may prevail under extreme stress or temperature conditions.
Intrinsic sluggish deformation kinetics of the HEA layers may also contribute to resistance to time-dependent deformation.
The proposed comparison decreases layer thickness while maintaining identical overall composition.
Failure to observe a statistically significant reduction in creep rate or strain accumulation at reduced layer thickness would falsify the hypothesis.
